passage: Every afternoon after lunch, the flat in Pune went quiet for a while. Five-year-old Eshaan used to hate it. 'Boring!' he'd moan, rolling on the rug. His father Tenzin didn't argue. He simply lay on the sofa with his own book while soft flute music played. One day Eshaan dragged his crayons over and drew a whole train, carriage by carriage. When the music ended he looked up, surprised. 'Papa, can quiet time be longer tomorrow?'

qa.q: What did Eshaan draw during quiet time?
qa.a: A whole train, carriage by carriage.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel about quiet time at first?
qa.a: He felt bored and fed up, moaning 'Boring!' and rolling on the rug.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin's approach work better than arguing?
qa.a: By resting with his own book and music, Tenzin showed quiet time was worth having, so Eshaan found his own calm activity.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see quiet time?
qa.a: Tenzin seems to see it as real rest, not laziness, which is why he joins in himself.

grounding: Shows a young child who learns to spend a short, calm time drawing to gentle music and finds it restful, with a parent who shows quiet time is not laziness.

passage:
'Jomon Sir, why is the light off here?'
'It's the resting corner, Devika. Just a short time. You can pick a book or listen to the rain music.'
'But I want to play blocks.'
'Blocks come after. Try the cushion first.'
Devika flopped onto the cushion and sighed loudly. 'This is lazy.'
'I sit in this corner too, at lunch. It helps me be a happy teacher.'
She opened a picture book about a sleepy whale. Soon she was tracing its tail with one finger.
The little bell tinkled.
'Already? Can I finish the whale?'
'Of course you can.'

qa.q: What was the picture book about?
qa.a: A sleepy whale.

qa.q: What did Devika think of the resting corner at first?
qa.a: She felt reluctant and thought it was lazy, sighing loudly because she wanted to play blocks.

qa.q: How did Jomon Sir help Devika give quiet time a try?
qa.a: He kept it short, offered choices and shared that he rests there too, showing that rest is valued.

qa.q: How does Jomon Sir seem to see rest?
qa.a: He sees it as something that helps even grown-ups, not as laziness.

grounding: Shows a young child discovering that a short spell with a book can be calm and restful, with a teacher who shows that rest is not laziness.

passage:
Class note, Nursery B, Tuesday
Deepak used to call our quiet corner 'the boring corner' and would roll around on the mat, poking friends. This week I tried something new: soft flute music, a basket of picture books and crayons, five minutes after lunch, with me sitting there too, reading my own book. On Monday he lasted two minutes. Today Deepak drew a whole kite, hummed along and asked, 'Can quiet time be longer tomorrow?' I said yes. I am making sure the children see me enjoying the rest too.
Nirmala

qa.q: What did Deepak draw today?
qa.a: A whole kite.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel about quiet time by the end of the week?
qa.a: He had come to enjoy it and felt calm and content, even asking for it to be longer.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala read a book during quiet time too?
qa.a: So the children could see an adult valuing and enjoying rest, instead of treating it as a punishment.

qa.q: How might Deepak's friends have felt once quiet time changed?
qa.a: They were probably relieved not to be poked and could enjoy the books and music in peace.

grounding: A teacher helps a young child discover that a short quiet time with books and music can be restful, and models valuing it.

passage: In the hill school above Kalimpong, Maria Miss rang a tiny bell after the midday meal. 'Quiet time,' she said, and opened the shutters to the mist. At first Pema hated it. She kicked the wall and asked every minute, 'Now can we play?' Maria Miss gave her a slate and chalk and sat nearby, drawing clouds herself. By the second week Pema was drawing yaks and humming. One afternoon, when the bell rang for games, Pema looked up and said, 'Wait, I'm not finished resting.'

qa.q: What did Maria Miss give Pema?
qa.a: A slate and chalk.

qa.q: What does Pema's line 'I'm not finished resting' show about how she feels now?
qa.a: She has come to feel calm and content in quiet time, no longer bored or restless.

qa.q: Why did it help that Maria Miss drew clouds herself?
qa.a: It showed that an adult enjoys quiet time too, so rest seemed worthwhile, not a punishment.

qa.q: What would change if Maria Miss had scolded Pema for kicking the wall?
qa.a: Pema might have learnt that quiet time is a punishment and kept fighting it instead of finding it restful.

grounding: A young child in a hill school learns that quiet time can be restful when an adult values it too.

passage: Every Sunday in their flat in Krakow, Rosa put on a record of soft piano and announced, 'Rest time.' Marek groaned and flopped over the sofa arm. 'Rest time is for babies!' Rosa didn't argue. She lay on the rug with her own book and set out paper and a jar of crayons beside her. Marek watched, then drew a tram, then a whole street of trams. When the record ended, he looked surprised. 'Already?' That evening he told his dad, 'Mama rests too. She isn't lazy. She's charging.'

qa.q: What did Marek draw during rest time?
qa.a: A tram, then a whole street of trams.

qa.q: How did Marek feel when the record ended?
qa.a: He felt surprised, having found the quiet time calm and pleasant rather than boring.

qa.q: Which choice made rest time work for Marek?
qa.a: Rosa didn't argue; she rested with her own book and set out crayons, showing that quiet time is worth enjoying.

qa.q: How might Marek's dad feel hearing Marek's comment?
qa.a: His dad would likely feel pleased and amused that Marek now sees rest as charging, not laziness.

grounding: A mother models quiet time so her young child discovers that calm can be restful rather than boring.

passage: After lunch at Sunflower Kindergarten, Nilesh sir dims the lights and puts on soft flute music. "Quiet time," he says. "Books, crayons or lying on the mat. Only whispers." On the first day Imran rolled around and said, "This is boring!" Nilesh sir didn't scold. He sat on the mat himself with a picture book and turned the pages slowly. By the second week Imran chose the crayons and drew a long, careful snake. When the music stopped, he looked up, surprised. "Already?" He stretched, yawned and smiled.

qa.q: What music does Nilesh sir put on during quiet time?
qa.a: Soft flute music.

qa.q: How had Imran's feelings about quiet time changed by the second week?
qa.a: He went from bored and restless to calm and absorbed, even surprised when it ended.

qa.q: How did Nilesh sir show that rest is valuable?
qa.a: He didn't scold, but joined in quietly with a book himself, showing quiet time as something he enjoys.

qa.q: What would change if Nilesh sir had scolded Imran on the first day?
qa.a: Imran might have seen quiet time as a punishment and fought it, instead of finding it restful.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to spend a short quiet time with crayons and music and finding it restful, with a teacher showing that rest is not laziness.
